memory_update.text: SYY should be retained as the reference benchmark for foodservice distribution scale, but not as the main underfollowed alpha candidate.
CHEF is the cleanest underfollowed public-market candidate for specialty restaurant distribution and center-of-the-plate procurement exposure.
WEST adds a less obvious B2B restaurant beverage-solutions angle; key survival tests are restaurant/foodservice mix, customer concentration, facility utilization, and free-cash-flow conversion.
FARM is a speculative shadow candidate below the preferred market-cap range; include only if the dashboard can tolerate micro-cap turnaround/liquidity risk and requires explicit falsification checks.

Need a later pass for USFD, PFGC, cold-storage/logistics providers, dairy/protein/produce suppliers, and restaurant procurement/software platforms; this pass was limited to four direct/reference names.
Keep SYY as the benchmark reference for broadline foodservice distribution scale, case volumes, procurement breadth, and inflation pass-through.
Prioritize CHEF in later layers as the cleaner underfollowed specialty-distribution candidate tied to upscale restaurants, specialty inputs, and center-of-plate procurement.
Track COLD as a second-order cold-chain infrastructure candidate, but require validation of foodservice versus retail/CPG exposure before assigning restaurant-theme purity.
Track FARM only as a speculative micro-cap exception due to direct restaurant/foodservice beverage distribution relevance, offset by turnaround, liquidity, and below-$300M market-cap risk.
Restaurant procurement scale can be vertically integrated inside franchisors, outsourced to broadline/specialty distributors, or embedded in cold-chain and route-density infrastructure.

Need a later pass for other public suppliers in proteins, dairy, produce logistics, bakery inputs, food packaging, cleaning/sanitation, and restaurant equipment that may have stronger chokepoint characteristics than distributors.
CHEF should remain in the restaurant distribution/procurement universe as a mid-cap specialty distributor with direct independent-restaurant, chef, specialty-SKU, and protein exposure.

WEST should remain as an underfollowed second-order candidate tied to B2B coffee, tea, extracts, ingredients, roasting, packaging, and distribution for foodservice and restaurant channels; needs financial-quality verification.

HFFG is a speculative shadow candidate because of sub-USD-300M market cap, but it has direct niche foodservice-distribution exposure to Asian restaurants, cold chain, seafood, specialty imports, produce, and packaging.

For restaurant themes, owned or controlled procurement and distribution can be an underappreciated profit and franchise-economics lever; Domino's supply-chain structure is a useful context anchor even though DPZ is not an underfollowed discovery candidate.

Layer 2 should verify gross-margin pass-through, route density, working-capital strain, food inflation sensitivity, customer concentration, supplier concentration, and whether specialty distributors have pricing power or merely commodity volume exposure.
PFGC should remain the reference benchmark for restaurant-facing foodservice distribution scale, supplier-cost pass-through, independent restaurant volumes, and route-density economics.

CHEF is a high-priority underfollowed candidate for the restaurant distribution node because its specialty and center-of-the-plate exposure maps directly to chef-driven restaurants and fragmented specialty procurement.

COLD is an adjacent cold-chain infrastructure candidate, not a restaurant pure play; further work must verify foodservice distributor and restaurant-linked customer exposure before upgrading the claim.

FARM is a speculative shadow candidate only: direct restaurant and foodservice DSD exposure is relevant, but micro-cap size, financial quality, liquidity, and restructuring risk require strict falsification.

Layer 2 should test whether distribution and procurement advantages show up in measurable indicators: gross margin resilience during inflation, delivery frequency, route density, customer retention, supplier concentration, and segment-level organic growth.
